text: The smallest positive integral value of $a$, for which all the roots of $x^{4}-ax^{2}+9=0$ are real and distinct, is equal to
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2026 (Online) 24th January Evening Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
Put $x^{2}=t$; the equation becomes $t^{2}-at+9=0$.

A positive root $t$ gives two distinct real roots $x=\pm \sqrt{t}$, while a negative $t$ gives no real $x$. So all four roots are real and distinct exactly when $t^{2}-at+9=0$ has two distinct positive roots.

Distinct real roots: $D=a^{2}-36>0\Rightarrow a<-6$ or $a>6$.

Both roots positive: their product is $9>0$, and their sum $a$ must be positive, so $a>0$.

Therefore $a>6$, and the smallest positive integer is $a=7$, for which $t=\dfrac{7\pm \sqrt{13}}{2}$, both positive and distinct.

Hence, the correct option is (A).

text:
Consider the following three statements for the function $f:(0,\infty )\to \mathrm{ℝ}$ defined by $f(x)=|\log _{e}x|-|x-1|$ :

(I) $f$ is differentiable at all $x>0$.

(II) $f$ is increasing in $(0,1)$.

(III) $f$ is decreasing in $(1,\infty )$.

Then.
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2026 (Online) 24th January Evening Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
Step 1: Write $f(x)$ without absolute values for different intervals

When $x\geq 1$, $\ln x$ is positive and $x-1$ is also positive. So:

$f(x)=|\ln x|-|x-1|=\ln x-(x-1)=\ln x-x+1$

for $x\geq 1$.

When $0<x<1$, $\ln x$ is negative and $x-1$ is negative. So:

$f(x)=|\ln x|-|x-1|=-\ln x-(-(x-1))=-\ln x+x-1$

for $0<x<1$.

So we can write:

$f(x)=\left \{\begin{array}{ll} \ln x-x+1 & \text{for}x\geq 1 \\  \\ -\ln x+x-1 & \text{for}0<x<1 \end{array} \right.$

Step 2: Find the derivative $f^{'}(x)$ in both cases

For $x\geq 1,$

$f^{'}(x)=\frac{d}{dx}(\ln x-x+1)=\frac{1}{x}-1$

For $0<x<1,$

$f^{'}(x)=\frac{d}{dx}(-\ln x+x-1)=-\frac{1}{x}+1$

So,

$f^{'}(x)=\left \{\begin{array}{ll} \frac{1}{x}-1 & \text{for}x\geq 1 \\  \\ -\frac{1}{x}+1 & \text{for}0<x<1 \end{array} \right.$

Step 3: Check differentiability at $x=1$

From the left of $x=1$:

$f^{'}(1^{-})=-\frac{1}{1}+1=0$

From the right of $x=1$:

$f^{'}(1^{+})=\frac{1}{1}-1=0$

Both one-sided derivatives are equal. So $f(x)$ is differentiable at $x=1$.

Since the formulas for $f^{'}(x)$ are valid everywhere for $x>0$, $f(x)$ is differentiable for all $x>0$.

Step 4: Check if $f(x)$ is increasing or decreasing

For $x>1$:

$f^{'}(x)=\frac{1}{x}-1$

Since $x>1$, $\frac{1}{x}<1$. So $f^{'}(x)<0$, which means $f(x)$ is decreasing for $x>1$.

For $0<x<1$:

$f^{'}(x)=-\frac{1}{x}+1$

Here, $\frac{1}{x}>1$, so $-\frac{1}{x}+1<0$, so $f^{'}(x)<0$. Therefore, $f(x)$ is decreasing for $0<x<1$ also.

Step 5: Check the statements

(I) $f$ is differentiable at all $x>0$: True

(II) $f$ is increasing in $(0,1)$: False

(III) $f$ is decreasing in $(1,\infty )$: True

So only statements (I) and (III) are correct.

text: Let $P=[p_{ij}]$ and $Q=[q_{ij}]$ be two square matrices of order 3 such that $q_{\mathrm{ij}}=2^{(\mathrm{i}+\mathrm{j}-1)}\mathrm{p}_{\mathrm{ij}}$ and $\det (\mathrm{Q})=2^{10}$. Then the value of $\det (\mathrm{adj}(\mathrm{adj}\mathrm{P}))$ is:

solution.body:
Given two $3\times 3$ matrices $P=[p_{ij}],Q=[q_{ij}]$ are given

$q_{ij}=2^{(i+j-1)}p_{ij},\det (Q)=2^{10}.$

To calculate $\det (\mathrm{adj}(\mathrm{adj}P))$

where $n$ is order of matrix which is 3

so, $\det (\mathrm{adj}(\mathrm{adj}P))=(\det (P))^{4}\ldots (1)$

Let P matrix

$P=\left [\begin{array}{lll} p_{11} & p_{12} & p_{13} \\ p_{21} & p_{22} & p_{23} \\ p_{31} & p_{32} & p_{33} \end{array}\right ]$

and $Q=\left [\begin{array}{lll} q_{11} & q_{12} & q_{13} \\ q_{21} & q_{22} & q_{23} \\ q_{31} & q_{32} & q_{33} \end{array}\right ]$

use $q_{ij}=2^{i+j-1}p_{ij}$ to find Q matrix

$\text{e.g.}q_{11}=2^{1+1-1}p_{11}=2p_{11},q_{23}=2^{2+3-1}p_{23}=2^{4}p_{23}$

$Q=\left [\begin{array}{lll} 2p_{11} & 2^{2}p_{12} & 2^{3}p_{13} \\ 2^{2}p_{21} & 2^{3}p_{22} & 2^{4}p_{23} \\ 2^{3}p_{31} & 2^{4}p_{32} & 2^{5}p_{33} \end{array}\right ]$

$\begin{array}{lllllll} Q=\left [\begin{array}{lll} 2p_{11} & 2^{2}p_{12} & 2^{3}p_{13} \\ 2^{2}p_{21} & 2^{3}p_{22} & 2^{4}p_{23} \\ 2^{3}p_{31} & 2^{4}p_{32} & 2^{5}p_{33} \end{array}\right ] \\ \det (Q)=\left |\begin{array}{lll} 2p_{11} & 2^{2}p_{12} & 2^{3}p_{13} \\ 2^{2}p_{21} & 2^{3}p_{22} & 2^{4}p_{23} \\ 2^{3}p_{31} & 2^{4}p_{32} & 2^{5}p_{33} \end{array}\right |=2^{10} \end{array}$

taking common 2 from $R_{1},2^{2}$ from $R_{2}&2^{3}$ from $R_{3}$

$\det (Q)=2\cdot 2^{2}\cdot 2^{3}\left |\begin{array}{lll} p_{11} & 2p_{12} & 2^{2}p_{13} \\ p_{21} & 2p_{22} & 2^{2}p_{23} \\ p_{31} & 2p_{32} & 2^{2}p_{33} \end{array}\right |=2^{10}$

taking common 2 from $C_{2}$ and $2^{2}$ from $C_{3}$

$2\cdot 2^{2}\cdot 2^{3}\cdot 2\cdot 2^{2}\left |\begin{array}{lll} p_{11} & p_{12} & p_{13} \\ p_{21} & p_{22} & p_{23} \\ p_{31} & p_{32} & p_{33} \end{array}\right |=2^{10}$

$\begin{array}{l} \Rightarrow 2^{9}\cdot \det (P)=2^{10} \\ \Rightarrow \det (P)=2 \\ \text{from}(1)\det (\mathrm{adj}(\mathrm{adj}P))=(\det (P))^{4}=2^{4}=16 \end{array}$

text: Let $y=y(x)$ be a differentiable function in the interval $(0,\infty )$ such that $y(1)=2$, and $\lim _{t\to x}\left (\frac{t^{2}y(x)-x^{2}y(t)}{x-t}\right )=3$ for each $x>0$. Then $2y(2)$ is equal to :
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2026 (Online) 24th January Evening Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
$\lim _{t\to x}\frac{t^{2}y(x)-x^{2}y(t)}{x-t}=3$

Substituting

$t\to x+h\Rightarrow h\to 0$

$\lim _{h\to 0}\frac{(x+h)^{2}y(x)-x^{2}y(x+h)}{-h}=3$

$f^{'}(x)=\lim _{h\to 0}\frac{f(x+h)-f(x)}{h}$

$\Rightarrow$ $\lim _{h\to 0}\frac{x^{2}y(x)+h^{2}y(x)+2xhy(x)-x^{2}y(x+h)}{-h}=3$

$\Rightarrow$ $\lim _{h\to 0}\frac{-x^{2}[y(x+h)-y(x)]+y(x)\left (h^{2}+2xh\right )}{-h}=3$

$\Rightarrow$ $\lim _{h\to 0}\frac{x^{2}[y(x+h)-y(x)]}{h}-\lim _{h\to 0}\frac{y(x)(h+2x)h}{h}=3$

Use

$f^{'}(x)=\lim _{h\to 0}\frac{f(x+h)-f(x)}{h}$

$x^{2}y^{'}(x)-2xy(x)=3$

Equation (1) is differential equation can be written by replacing

$y^{'}(x)=\frac{dy}{dx}\text{and}y(x)=y$

$\Rightarrow$ $x^{2}\frac{dy}{dx}-2xy=3$

$\Rightarrow$ $\frac{dy}{dx}-\frac{2}{x}y=\frac{3}{x^{2}}$ (Linear differential equation)

Integrating factor

$\text{I.F}=e^{\int -\frac{2}{x}dx}=e^{-2\ln x}=e^{\ln \left (\frac{1}{x2}\right )}=\frac{1}{x^{2}}$

$\therefore$ Solution of linear differential equation

$y\cdot (\text{I.F})=\int (\text{I.F})\cdot \frac{3}{x^{2}}dx$

$\Rightarrow$ $y\cdot \frac{1}{x^{2}}=\int \frac{1}{x^{2}}\cdot \frac{3}{x^{2}}dx=\int \frac{3}{x^{4}}dx$

$\Rightarrow$ $\frac{y}{x^{2}}=3\times \frac{x^{-4+1}}{-4+1}=-\frac{1}{x^{3}}+C$

$\Rightarrow$ $y=-\frac{1}{x}+Cx^{2}$ (General solution)

Apply initial condition

$y(1)=2$

$\Rightarrow2=-\frac{1}{1}+C(1)\Rightarrow C=3$

So particular solution is : $y(x)=-\frac{1}{x}+3x^{2}$

$\therefore$ $y(2)=-\frac{1}{2}+3(2)^{2}=12-\frac{1}{2}=\frac{23}{2}$

$\Rightarrow$ $2y(2)=23$

text: The sum of all values of $α$, for which the shortest distance between the lines $\frac{x+1}{α}=\frac{y-2}{-1}=\frac{z-4}{-α}$ and $\frac{x}{α}=\frac{y-1}{2}=\frac{z-1}{2α}$ is $\sqrt{2}$, is
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2026 (Online) 24th January Evening Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
Lines into vector form

$\begin{array}{l} L_{1}:⃗{r}=-\hat{i}+2\hat{j}+4\hat{k}+λ(α\hat{i}-\hat{j}-α\hat{k}) \\ L_{2}:⃗{r}=\hat{j}+\hat{k}+μ(α\hat{i}+2\hat{j}+2α\hat{k}) \end{array}$

Lines are not parallel because direction ratios are not proportional

$\frac{α}{α}\neq \frac{-1}{2}$

So lines are skew lines.

Minimum distance between two skew lines $⃗{r}=⃗{a}+λ⃗{b}$ and $⃗{r}=⃗{c}+μ⃗{d}$ is given as

$d=\left |\frac{(⃗{a}-⃗{c})\cdot (⃗{b}\times ⃗{d})}{|⃗{b}\times ⃗{b}|}\right |$

$⃗{a}=-\hat{i}+2\hat{j}+4\hat{k},⃗{c}=\hat{j}+\hat{k}$

$⃗{b}=α\hat{i}-\hat{j}-α\hat{k},⃗{d}=α\hat{i}+2\hat{j}+2α\hat{k}$

$⃗{b}\times ⃗{d}=\left |\begin{array}{lll} \hat{i} & \hat{j} & \hat{k} \\ α & -1 & -α \\ α & 2 & 2α \end{array}\right |$

$=\hat{i}(-2α+2α)-\hat{j}\left (2α^{2}+α^{2}\right )+\hat{k}(2α+α)$

$\therefore$ $⃗{b}\times ⃗{d}=-3α^{2}\hat{j}+3α\hat{k}$

$\Rightarrow$ $|⃗{b}\times ⃗{d}|=\sqrt{9α^{4}+9α^{2}}$

$\Rightarrow$ $⃗{a}-⃗{c}=-\hat{i}+\hat{j}+3\hat{k}$

$\Rightarrow$ $\left |\frac{(⃗{a}-⃗{c})\cdot (⃗{b}\times ⃗{d})}{|⃗{b}\times ⃗{d}|}\right |=\sqrt{2}$

$\Rightarrow$ $\left |\frac{(-\hat{i}+\hat{j}+3\hat{k})\cdot \left (-3α^{2}\hat{j}+3α\hat{k}\right )}{\sqrt{9α^{4}+9α^{2}}}\right |=\sqrt{2}$

$\Rightarrow$ $\left |\frac{-3α^{2}+9α}{3\sqrt{α^{4}+α^{2}}}\right |=\sqrt{2}$

$\Rightarrow$ $\left |\frac{-3α(α-3)}{3α\sqrt{α^{2}+1}}\right |=\sqrt{2}$

$\Rightarrow$ $\left |\frac{α-3}{\sqrt{1+α^{2}}}\right |=\sqrt{2}$

squaring

$\Rightarrow$ $\frac{(α-3)^{2}}{1+α^{2}}=2$

$\Rightarrow$ $α^{2}+9-6α=2+2α^{2}$

$\Rightarrow$ $α^{2}+6α-7=0$

This equation has two roots say $α_{1}$ and $α_{2}$

So, sum of roots $=-\frac{\text{coefficient of}α}{\text{coefficient of}α^{2}}$

$\therefore$ $α_{1}+α_{2}=-6$

$f(x)=\left \{\begin{array}{ll} b^{2}\sin \left (\frac{π}{2}\left [\frac{π}{2}(\cos x+\sin x)\cos x\right ]\right ), & x<0 \\ \frac{\sin x-\frac{1}{2}\sin 2x}{x^{3}} & ,x>0 \\ a & ,x=0 \end{array} \right.$

is continuous at $x=0$, then $a^{2}+b^{2}$ is equal to :
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2026 (Online) 24th January Evening Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
It is given that $f(x)$ is continuous at $x=0$

This means at $x=0$

L.H.L = R.H.L = f(0) = a

Calculating L.H.L using the definition of $f(x)$ for $x<0$

$\lim _{x\to 0^{-}}f(x)=\lim _{x\to 0}b^{2}\sin \left (\frac{π}{2}\left [\frac{π}{2}(\cos x+\sin x)\cos x\right ]\right )=a$

$\Rightarrow$ $\lim _{x\to 0}b^{2}\sin \left (\frac{π}{2}\left [\frac{π}{2}\left (\cos ^{2}x+\frac{\sin 2x}{2}\right )\right ]\right )=a$

$\begin{array}{l} \cos ^{2}\left (0^{-}\right )=1^{-}\text{Less than}1 \\ \sin 2\left (0^{-}\right )=0^{-}\text{Less than}0 \\ \Rightarrow a=b^{2}\sin \left (\dfrac{π}{2}\left [\dfrac{3.14}{2}\left (1^{-}+0^{-}\right )\right ]\right ) \end{array}$

$\Rightarrow$ $a=b^{2}\sin \left (\frac{π}{2}[1.57(1^{-})]\right )$

$\Rightarrow$ $a=b^{2}\sin \left (\frac{π}{2}\left [1.57^{-}\right ]\right ),\left [1.57^{-}\right ]=1\{[t]\to$ G.I.F $\}$

$\Rightarrow$ $a=b^{2}\sin \left (\frac{π}{2}\times 1\right )=b^{2}$

Calculating R.H.L using the function definition for $x>0$

$\lim _{x\to 0^{+}}f(x)=\lim _{x\to 0^{+}}\frac{\sin x-\frac{1}{2}\sin 2x}{x^{3}}=a$

$\Rightarrow$ $\lim _{x\to 0^{+}}\frac{\sin x-\frac{1}{2}\times 2\sin x\cos x}{x^{3}}=a$

$\Rightarrow$ $\lim _{x\to 0^{+}}\frac{\sin x(1-\cos x)}{x\cdot x^{2}}=a$

Using limits result $\lim _{x\to 0}\frac{\sin x}{x}=1$ and $\lim _{x\to 0}\frac{1-\cos x}{x^{2}}=\frac{1}{2}$

Putting these results

$a=1\cdot \frac{1}{2}=\frac{1}{2}$

So $a^{2}+b^{2}=a^{2}+a\left \{b^{2}=a \right.$ from $L.H.L\}$

$=\frac{1}{4}+\frac{1}{2}=\frac{3}{4}$

solution.body:
$Y=\{ax+b:x\in X\}.\text{and}X=\{x\in \mathrm{ℕ}:1\leq x\leq 19\}$

mean for $Y$ is 30. 

$\therefore$ $(\bar{Y}=30)$

$\Rightarrow$ $\frac{\sum\limits _{i=1}^{19}(ax_{i}+b)^{2}}{19}-(30)^{2}=750$

$\Rightarrow$ $\sum\limits _{i=1}^{19}\left (a^{2}x_{i}^{2}+b^{2}+2abx_{i}\right )=(750+900)19$

$\Rightarrow$ $a^{2}\sum\limits _{i=1}^{19}x_{i}^{2}+\sum\limits _{i=1}^{19}b^{2}+2ab\sum\limits _{i=1}^{19}x_{i}=1650\times 19$

$\Rightarrow$ $a^{2}\left (1^{2}+2^{2}+\cdots +19^{2}\right )+\sum\limits _{i=1}^{19}b^{2}+2ab(1+2+\cdots +19)=1650\times 19$

$\Rightarrow$ $a^{2}\cdot \frac{19\times 20\times 39}{6}+19b^{2}+\frac{2ab\times 19\times 20}{2}=1650\times 19$

$\Rightarrow$ $130a^{2}+b^{2}+20ab=1650$ ......(2)

Substitute value of $a$ from (1) in equation (2)

$130\left (\frac{30-b}{10}\right )^{2}+b^{2}+20b\left (\frac{30-b}{10}\right )=1650$

$\Rightarrow$ $\frac{13}{10}\left (900+b^{2}-60b\right )+b^{2}+60b-2b^{2}=1650$

$\Rightarrow$ $11700+13b^{2}-780b+10b^{2}+600b-20b^{2}=16500$

$\Rightarrow$ $3b^{2}-180b-4800=0$

$\Rightarrow$ $b^{2}-60b-1600=0$

Let roots of quadratic equation is $b_{1},b_{2}$ 

So sum of possible values of $b=$ sum of roots

$b_{1}+b_{2}=\frac{-\text{coefficient of}b}{\text{coefficient of}b^{2}}=60$

text: The largest value of $n$, for which $40^{n}$ divides $60!$, is
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2026 (Online) 24th January Evening Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
To find largest value of $n$ for which 60 ! is divisible by $40^{n}$

This means we need to find exponent of 40 in 60 !

$40=2^{3}\times 5$

Key Concept: formula for exponent of prime $p$ in $k!$ is given as $\left [\frac{k}{p}\right ]+\left [\frac{k}{p^{2}}\right ]+\left [\frac{k}{p^{3}}\right ]+\ldots$ where [] is greatest integer function.

so, exponent of 2 in 60 !

$\begin{array}{l} \left [\dfrac{60}{2}\right ]+\left [\dfrac{60}{2^{2}}\right ]+\left [\dfrac{60}{2^{3}}\right ]+\left [\dfrac{60}{2^{4}}\right ]+\left [\dfrac{60}{2^{5}}\right ]+\left [\dfrac{60}{2^{6}}\right ]+\ldots  \\ 30+15+7+3+1=56-\text{(1)} \end{array}$

exponent of 5 in 60 !

$\begin{array}{l} \left [\dfrac{60}{5}\right ]+\left [\dfrac{60}{5^{2}}\right ]+\left [\dfrac{60}{5^{3}}\right ]+\ldots  \\ 12+2+0\cdots =14-(2) \end{array}$

Combining (1) and (2)

60 ! is divisible by $2^{56}\times 5^{14}\times N$, where $N$ is natural number.

60 ! is divisible by $4\times \left (2^{3}\right )^{18}\times 5^{14}\times N$

60 ! is divisible by $4\times \left (2^{3}\right )^{4}\times \left (2^{3}\right )^{14}\times 5^{14}\times N$

$60!$ is divisible by $2^{14}\times 40^{14}\times N$

text: The number of elements in the set $\{x\in [0,180^{\circ }]:\tan (x+100^{\circ })=\tan (x+50^{\circ })\tan x\tan (x-50^{\circ })\}$ is $____$ .
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2026 (Online) 24th January Evening Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
$\begin{array}{l} \begin{array}{l} \tan (x+100^{\circ })=\tan (x+50^{\circ })\tan x\tan (x-50^{\circ });x\in [0,180^{\circ }] \\ \dfrac{\tan (x+100^{\circ })}{\tan x}=\tan (x+50^{\circ })\tan (x-50^{\circ }) \\ \dfrac{\sin (x+100^{\circ })\cdot \cos x}{\cos (x+100^{\circ })\cdot \sin x}=\dfrac{\sin (x+50^{\circ })\sin (x-50^{\circ })}{\cos (x+50^{\circ })\cos (x-50^{\circ })} \end{array} \\ \text{Apply Componendo and Dividendo rule} \\ \begin{array}{l} \dfrac{\sin (x+100^{\circ })\cos x+\cos (x+100^{\circ })\sin x}{\sin (x+100^{\circ })\cos x-\cos (x+100^{\circ })\sin x}=\dfrac{\sin (x+50^{\circ })\sin (x-50^{\circ })+\cos (x-50^{\circ })\cos (x+50^{\circ })}{\sin (x+50^{\circ })\sin (x-50^{\circ })-\cos (x+50^{\circ })\cos (x-50^{\circ })} \\ \text{use}\sin A\cos B\pm \cos A\sin B=\sin (A\pm B)\text{and}\cos A\cos B\pm \sin A\sin B=\cos (A\mp B) \\ \dfrac{\sin (x+100^{\circ }+x)}{\sin (x+100^{\circ }-x)}=\dfrac{\cos [(x+50^{\circ })-(x-50^{\circ })]}{-\cos [(x+50^{\circ })+(x-50^{\circ })]} \\ \dfrac{\sin (2x+100^{\circ })}{\sin 100^{\circ }}=\dfrac{\cos 100^{\circ }}{-\cos 2x} \end{array} \end{array}$

$\begin{array}{l} \dfrac{\sin (90^{\circ }+(2x+10^{\circ }))}{\sin (90^{\circ }+10^{\circ })}=\dfrac{\cos (90^{\circ }+10^{\circ })}{-\cos 2x} \\ \dfrac{\cos (2x+10^{\circ })}{\cos 10^{\circ }}=\dfrac{-\sin 10^{\circ }}{-\cos 2x} \\ \cos (2x+10^{\circ })\cos 2x=\sin 10^{\circ }\cos 10^{\circ } \\ 2\cos (2x+10^{\circ })\cos 2x=2\sin 10^{\circ }\cos 10^{\circ } \\ 2\cos (2x+10^{\circ })\cos 2x=\sin 20^{\circ } \\ \cos (4x+10^{\circ })+\cos 10^{\circ }=\sin 20^{\circ } \\ \cos (4x+10^{\circ })=\sin 20^{\circ }-\cos 10^{\circ } \\ \cos (4x+10^{\circ })=\sin 20^{\circ }-\sin 80^{\circ }\{\cos 10^{\circ }=\sin (90^{\circ }-10^{\circ })\} \\ =2\cos 50^{\circ }\sin (-30^{\circ }) \\ =-2\cos 50^{\circ }\times \dfrac{1}{2}=-\cos 50^{\circ }=\cos (180^{\circ }-50^{\circ }) \\ \cos (4x+10^{\circ })=\cos 130^{\circ } \end{array}$

$\begin{array}{l} 4x+10^{\circ }=2nπ\pm 130^{\circ },n\in I \\ 4x+10^{\circ }=360^{\circ }n\pm 130^{\circ },n\in I \\ 4x+10^{\circ }=360^{\circ }n+130^{\circ }\text{or}4x+10^{\circ }=360^{\circ }n-130^{\circ } \\ 4x=360^{\circ }n+120^{\circ }\text{or}4x=360^{\circ }n-140^{\circ } \end{array}$

$\begin{array}{l} \begin{array}{l} x=\dfrac{360^{\circ }n+120^{\circ }}{4} \\ n=0,x=30^{\circ } \\ n=1,x=\dfrac{480^{\circ }}{4}=120^{\circ } \\ n=2,x=\dfrac{360^{\circ }\times 2+120^{\circ }}{4} \\ x=210^{\circ } \end{array} \\ \begin{array}{l} x=\dfrac{360^{\circ }n-140^{\circ }}{4} \\ n=1,x=\dfrac{360^{\circ }-140^{\circ }}{4}=\dfrac{220^{\circ }}{4}=55^{\circ } \\ n=2,x=\dfrac{360^{\circ }\times 2-140^{\circ }}{4}=\dfrac{580^{\circ }}{4}=145^{\circ } \\ n=3,x=\dfrac{360^{\circ }\times 3-140^{\circ }}{4}=\dfrac{940^{\circ }}{4}=235^{\circ } \end{array} \end{array}$

for $x\in [0,180^{\circ }]$ solutions are

$x=30^{\circ },55^{\circ },120^{\circ },145^{\circ }$

so, total number of solutions are $=4$ Ans

text: Let $(h,k)$ lie on the circle $\mathrm{C}:x^{2}+y^{2}=4$ and the point $(2h+1,3k+2)$ lie on an ellipse with eccentricity $e$. Then the value of $\frac{5}{e^{2}}$ is equal to $____$ .
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2026 (Online) 24th January Evening Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
$(\mathrm{h},\mathrm{k})$ lie on circle $x^{2}+y^{2}=4$.

so, $h^{2}+k^{2}=4--$ (1)

$(2h+1,3k+2)$ lies on ellipse This means $x=2h+1$ and $y=3k+2$ lies on ellipse

Substitute $\mathrm{h}=\frac{x-1}{2}$ and $\mathrm{k}=\frac{y-2}{3}$ in equation (1)

$\begin{array}{l} \left (\dfrac{x-1}{2}\right )^{2}+\left (\dfrac{y-2}{3}\right )^{2}=4 \\ \dfrac{(x-1)^{2}}{16}+\dfrac{(y-2)^{2}}{36}=1 \end{array}$

This is shifted ellipse of the form $\frac{(x-x_{1})^{2}}{a^{2}}+\frac{(y-y_{1})^{2}}{b^{2}}=1$, $\mathrm{a}=4,\mathrm{b}=6$

eccentricity e $=\sqrt{1-\frac{a^{2}}{b^{2}}}=\sqrt{1-\frac{16}{36}}=\sqrt{\frac{5}{9}}$

$e^{2}=\frac{5}{9}⟹\frac{5}{e^{2}}=9$ Ans

text: If $f(x)$ satisfies the relation $f(x)=e^{x}+\int\limits _{0}^{1}(y+xe^{x})f(y)dy$, then $e+f(0)$ is equal to $____$ .
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2026 (Online) 24th January Evening Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
The integration is with respect to $y$, so $x$ and $e^{x}$ come out of the integral:

$f(x)=e^{x}+\int\limits _{0}^{1}yf(y)dy+xe^{x}\int\limits _{0}^{1}f(y)dy$

With the constants $A=\int\limits _{0}^{1}yf(y)dy$ and $B=\int\limits _{0}^{1}f(y)dy$,

$f(x)=e^{x}+A+Bxe^{x}$

Integrating this over $[0,1]$ and using $\int ye^{y}dy=e^{y}(y-1)$:

$B=\int\limits _{0}^{1}(e^{y}+A+Bye^{y})dy=(e-1)+A+B[e^{y}(y-1)]_{0}^{1}=(e-1)+A+B$

So $A=1-e$.

Then $f(0)=1+A=2-e$, and $e+f(0)=2$.

Hence, the answer is 2.
